Issued at 429 AM CDT Fri Aug 21 2026

Northwest flow aloft continues over the Northern Plains early 
this morning while the upstream western CONUS ridge is beginning
to become more amplified. A shortwave embedded in the northwest
flow is depicted on water vapor imagery over southern 
Saskatchewan and is forecast to move from northwest to southeast
North Dakota through this afternoon. Scattered showers have 
been ongoing with this wave since late last evening, and most 
guidance suggests these will hold together at least until 
reaching central North Dakota around midday. A couple of CAMs 
have hinted at a strong thunderstorm between the Missouri and 
James River Valleys this afternoon, but it is difficult to find 
model support for CAPE higher than 100-200 J/kg. An occasional 
brief thunderstorm cannot be ruled out at any point with this 
activity, but the probability of lightning is not high enough 
to carry a mention in the forecast. 

The surface pattern this morning is very benign, with broad 
ridging extending from Alberta/Saskatchewan through the 
Missouri River Valley. Shallow fog has developed from near the 
Turtle Mountains to the northern James River Valley and back 
west towards Lake Sakakawea. The fog could reduce visibility in
low lying areas before clearing by mid morning. The high 
temperature forecast for today is similar to what was observed 
yesterday, generally ranging from the upper 70s far north to 
upper 80s far southwest. The center of the surface high pressure
will become more focused over Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and into 
North Dakota tonight. NBM spread for low temperatures tonight 
is small, but would not be surprised to see colder percentiles 
in the 40s verify. On Saturday, the surface high/ridge slides 
into the Red River Valley as the highly-amplified upper level 
ridge begins to shift off the Northern Rockies. Highs on 
Saturday are projected to remain similar or be just a touch 
cooler at most locations, with mid 70s to mid 80s.

Shortwave energy preceding a potent Pacific Northwest upper low
will begin ejecting off the Northern Rockies Saturday night. 
The Pacific Northwest low will push the upper ridge axis into 
the High Plains, but with embedded shortwave energy and 
underlying moisture return. Recent consensus guidance has 
trended to a slower progression of the synoptic scale wave 
pattern, but the NBM has actually refined PoPs to higher 
percentages and a more focused corridor moving from southwest 
North Dakota early Sunday morning to northwest-south central 
North Dakota Sunday afternoon. Model soundings show strong 
capping, and deterministic guidance would suggest QPF outpacing
a ribbon of higher CAPE. Therefore, any convection during the 
day Sunday is favored to remain elevated, with a very low risk 
for severe weather. Medium shower and thunderstorm chances 
(around 30 to 60 percent) expand across all of western and 
central North Dakota Sunday evening. But despite increasing 
buoyancy, even for elevated parcels, confidence in any severe 
threat through Sunday remains low. Monday could be a different 
story though if the slower progression of the potent upper low 
comes to fruition. Ensembles now favor an occlusion of the low 
over Saskatchewan on Monday, with the primary surface frontal 
boundary attendant to the low moving through western and 
central North Dakota during the day. The environment downstream
of the surface front could become supportive of severe 
thunderstorms, with CAPE as high as 2000 J/kg and deep layer 
shear around 35 to 45 kts. But there is still too much 
uncertainty in forecast details to begin messaging a severe 
threat at this time. The post-frontal air mass could become 
hot, dry, and breezy, which may lead to near-critical fire 
weather conditions in western North Dakota Monday afternoon. 

The occluded low is forecast to track southeastward, reaching 
the Great Lakes late Wednesday. In its wake, the upper ridge is 
forecast to rebound from the Southern Rockies through the 
Northern High Plains ahead of another potent trough digging 
into the Pacific Northwest. Ensemble spread grows by the end of 
next week, but there are hints that the Pacific Northwest 
trough could break down the ridge and transition flow aloft to 
quasi-zonal. A slight warmup continues to be advertised for 
Sunday and Monday, with highs reaching the lower 80s to lower 
90s, followed by a return to near or slightly below 
temperatures that could last through the rest of next week.
